## Part 1 – Load Required Libraries

-   In this assignment, we use several R packages to perform text mining, sentiment analysis, data manipulation, and visualization.

    ```{r}
    #| label: Required Libraries

    # Load required libraries

    library(tidyverse)
    library(tidytext)
    library(janeaustenr)
    library(stringr)
    library(wordcloud)
    library(RColorBrewer)

    ```

-   Explanation of the packages:

    -   tidyverse: Data manipulation and visualization

    -   tidytext: Text mining and sentiment analysis

    -   janeaustenr: Provides Jane Austen's books

    -   stringr: Text processing and regular expressions

    -   wordcloud: Creates word cloud visualizations

    -   RColorBrewer: Provides color palettes

## Part 2 – Data Preparation: Loading the Dataset

-   Data Preparation

    -   In this section, we load Jane Austen's books using the `janeaustenr` package and explore the available dataset. We will identify the different books and examine the structure of the text data.

    ```{r}
    #| label: Load Dataset

    # Load Jane Austen's books
    austen_data <- austen_books()

    # Display the first six rows
    head(austen_data)


    ```

-   Explanation:

    -   austen_books() loads the collection of Jane Austen's novels.
    -   We store the dataset in an object called austen_data.
    -   head() displays the first six rows so we can inspect the data.

-   Explore the available books

    -   The unique() function identifies the distinct book titles in the dataset. This allows us to confirm that Emma is included.

```{r}
#| label: Explore the available books

# Display all available book titles
unique(austen_data$book)

```

-   Examine the dataset structure
    -   glimpse() shows the columns and data types.
    -   count(book) calculates how many text lines are available for each novel.

```{r}
#| label: Dataset Structure

# Examine the structure of the dataset
glimpse(austen_data)

# Count the number of lines for each book
austen_data %>%
  count(book)

```

## Part 3 – Extracting Emma and Chapter Detection

-   In this section, we extract Jane Austen's novel Emma from the complete dataset. We then use regular expressions to identify chapter headings and assign line numbers and chapter numbers to the text.

```{r}
#| label: Extracting Emma and chapter detection

# Extract Emma and identify chapter boundaries

emma <- austen_data %>%
  filter(book == "Emma") %>%
  mutate(
    linenumber = row_number(),
    chapter = cumsum(
      str_detect(
        text,
        regex("^chapter [\\divxlc]", ignore_case = TRUE)
      )
    )
  )

# Display the first few rows
head(emma)

```

-   Explanation of the code:

    -   filter(): Selects only the novel Emma.
    -   mutate(): Creates new columns.
    -   row_number(): Assigns a sequential number to each line.
    -   str_detect(): Detects chapter headings using a regular expression.
    -   regex(): Makes chapter detection case-insensitive.
    -   cumsum(): Increments the chapter number whenever a chapter heading is detected.
    -   The regular expression "\^chapter \[\\divxlc\]": looks for lines beginning with the word "Chapter" followed by a Roman numeral or digit.

-   Check the chapter numbers

    -   This helps verify that the chapter identification worked.

```{r}
#| label: Check Chapter Numbers

# Check the number of chapters
max(emma$chapter)

# Count lines in each chapter
emma %>%
  count(chapter)

```

-   Check the dataset structure

```{r}
#| label: Data structure check 2

# Examine the prepared Emma dataset
glimpse(emma)

# Display the first 10 rows
emma %>%
  select(book, linenumber, chapter, text) %>%
  head(10)

```
